caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Turkey's public debt is low and falling: 44.2% of GDP in 2006 (the series high), 38.3% in 2020, 29.4% in 2022, and a projected series low of 23.5% in 2025. The paradox is that low sovereign debt coexists with chronic macro instability — the vulnerabilities are private-sector FX debt, the current account, and inflation, not the sovereign balance sheet. GDP grew from $554.9bn in 2006 to a projected $1,597.3bn in 2025. The state's borrowing is modest; the risk is that a currency crisis forces contingent liabilities onto the sovereign, as quasi-fiscal schemes (like the FX-protected deposit program) have done.
inflation_management: Turkey is the textbook case of unorthodox monetary policy's costs. Inflation was 6.2% in 2009 (the low), 12.3% in 2020, then exploded to 72.3% in 2022, the series high, after the central bank cut rates into rising inflation on political direction — the lira collapsed. It was still 58.5% in 2024 and is projected at 34.9% for 2025: disinflation under the post-2023 orthodox turn (aggressive hikes under a new economic team), but far from target. Central-bank independence was effectively suspended 2018-23; credibility is being rebuilt but the 2022-24 episode destroyed years of anchoring.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis; Turkey recovered fast on credit-fueled growth.
Lira crisis (2018): the currency collapsed as the central bank resisted hiking; inflation took off.
Unorthodox policy experiment: rate cuts into 70%+ inflation (2021-23) produced the 72.3% peak in 2022.
Orthodox turn (mid-2023): new economic team hiked rates aggressively; disinflation began.
Inflation projected at 34.9% — falling but still the highest in the G20; debt at a series low of 23.5% of GDP.

outlook_next_decade: Turkey's outlook hinges on whether the orthodox turn holds through the political cycle: disinflation from 72.3% to a projected 34.9% is real progress, but credibility is fragile and the 2028 election cycle is the test. The structural vulnerabilities — energy import dependence, private FX debt, the current-account deficit — are unchanged. Low public debt is a genuine buffer. The honest analytical assessment: the direction is right, the destination (single-digit inflation) is years away, and political risk is the dominant variable.
